title: What every AI engineer needs to know about GPUs — Charles Frye, Modal
talk_summary: Charles Frye explains GPU hardware economics for AI engineers: hardware now scales bandwidth, not latency, and the tensor core (low-precision matrix-matrix multiply) is the only part getting dramatically faster. The practical payoff is that many cheap samples from a small model plus a verifier can match a large model, because batching turns memory-bound decoding into compute-bound matrix-matrix work.

takeaways.technique: Best-of-N sampling with a verifier instead of a bigger model
takeaways.what_they_do: Run a small model many times on the same prompt, load weights once, and use a programmatic verifier (e.g. Python tests) to pick the winning output.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can use llama 318B to match GPT40 with like a 100 Yeah, 100 generations
takeaways.numbers: Llama 3.1 8B with ~100 generations + test verifier reportedly matches GPT-4o

takeaways.technique: Prefer small models scaled out over one large model
takeaways.what_they_do: Argue that small open models are now good enough that scaling out cheap generations beats paying for a frontier model, especially when a verifier exists.
takeaways.evidence_quote: maybe I can get away with running a smaller model that fits on a GPU that's under my desk um uh and then I just like scale it out

takeaways.technique: Batch identical prompts to amortize weight loads
takeaways.what_they_do: When decoding is memory-bound, reuse one weight load across many generations of the same prompt to convert the workload into compute-bound matrix-matrix math.
takeaways.evidence_quote: run it like a thousand times on the same prompt now you're loading the weights and you only load the weights one time

takeaways.what_they_do: Use an objective checker (tests) as the selector among many candidate outputs, rather than trusting a single model judgment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you have a good verifier either, in this case, this is does it pass a Python test
